doc.title: Anat Cohen interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, September 9, 2021

title: Playing after Paquito D'Rivera and recording 'And the World Weeps'
summary: She treats following Paquito as a positive challenge, and describes his recording on Claroscuro and his inspiration to her.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Who were the great clarinetists? Favorites and rivals

blocks.x: Thanks for sharing that. I love that story. And speaking of important people the tune with Paquito D’Rivera was called “And the World Weeps.” And I’ve been in a situation a couple of times in my life where I was playing next to someone I really admired or was a mentor or teacher. And I was wondering if you were thinking, because he soloed first, and beautifully, did you allow yourself to have these kind of somewhat negative thoughts like what am I going to do now? You know I would have done what he did but he already did it. Or it sounds like maybe you don’t let those kind of things get into your head.

I just, you know I just have a different approach because what would I do now, for me, is a positive thought, not a negative thought. Because if he played something and he left me to a point, say a challenge, what do I have to add? How can I add to the music after everything that he already gave? So for me it’s not like oh my God he played so beautiful now I’m going to — I mean there’s no time and no room for negative thoughts at this point, it’s only about think about the music and you have to really be — sometimes go into something that maybe you haven’t tried yet. Maybe I haven’t played before but the moment wants something else. So that’s what I’m saying if I was planning what I’m going to play and then Paquito has played it I would be like — not be in the moment and not be able to add anything because I would be all confused. So you know, but Paquito is © Fillius Jazz Archive -7-

definitely somebody I admire so much and it was such a thrill to have him, it was the D.C. Jazz Festival and actually he recorded that tune with me on my album Ciaroscuro, that “And the World Weeps.” It’s a Dr. Lonnie Smith song, a very simple minor eight bars, the song is just powerful and simple like many songs. And it’s just great because it can really show how for me how to be connected with your soul and how the clarinet can be so expressive and get such a wide range of emotions. And Pacquito is such an inspiration, the way he plays the clarinet, his sound on the clarinet, the kind of genres and music he dives into and what he presents in one show. And for somebody that was, you know I moved to New York and I was all confused about, oh I want to do this music or that music, how do you play — he’s a person that combines his classical roots with his love for Brazilian music with his Cuban roots to love of Argentinean music, for the world traveler, and he makes it be one thing and it was very inspiring for me to say hold on, I connect all of those things. It’s not — the music might be different from different places but the way we’re going to be playing it with the band we’re going to make it ours. So he was inspiring.
